'''Arverne''' is a neighborhood in the [[New York City]] [[Boroughs of New York City|borough]] of [[Queens]], on the [[Rockaway, Queens|Rockaway Peninsula]]. It was initially developed by [[Remington Vernam (land developer)|Remington Vernam]], whose signature "R. Vernam" inspired the name of the neighborhood.<ref>{{cite news |title=On the Beach, a Brand New Life |first=Jeff |last=Vandam |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/02/13/nyregion/thecity/13arve.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=February 13, 2005 |access-date=October 2, 2007 |quote=His wife names the area Arverne because he signs his checks ''R. Vernam'' |archive-date=May 7, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140507013259/http://www.nytimes.com/2005/02/13/nyregion/thecity/13arve.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Arverne extends from Beach 54th Street to Beach 79th Street, along its main thoroughfare [[Beach Channel Drive]], alternatively known as Rev. Joseph H. May Drive.

Arverne is located in [[Queens Community Board 14|Queens Community District 14]] and its ZIP Code is 11692.<ref name="NYCPlanning"/> It is patrolled by the [[New York City Police Department]]'s 100th Precinct.

==History==

=== Original settlement ===
[[File:Arverne, NY.jpg|thumb|Overhead view of Arverne]]
Vernam's original plan was to name the neighborhood Arverne-by-the-Sea. One grandiose plan, influenced by his wife Florence, included a canal running through the neighborhood, reminiscent of the [[Amstel]] canal in [[Amsterdam]], the [[Netherlands]]. When this plan fell through, the canal right-of-way was converted into a thoroughfare, Amstel Boulevard, which, except for a stub west of Beach 71st Street, was later incorporated into Beach Channel Drive.

Located on the [[Rockaway Boardwalk]], Arverne became well known as a beachfront community with inexpensive summer bungalows,  hotels of varying expense and luxury, and amusements and [[boardwalk (entertainment district)|boardwalk]] concessions. It also attracted year-round residents. On January 3, 1914, a storm devastated the peninsula's neighborhoods and swept the 1,200-seat Arverne Pier Theater out to sea.<ref>''[[The Wave of Long Island]]'', January 10, 1914, p. 1</ref> On June 15, 1922, a fire leveled a large part of Arverne, leaving about 10,000 people homeless, although the neighborhood was quick to rebuild.<ref>{{cite news |title=400 Buildings Burned at Arverne; 10,000 Made Homeless; 60 Injured, Loss $4,000,000 in Half Square Mile |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=June 16, 1922 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1922/06/16/archives/400-buildings-burned-at-arverne-10000-made-homeless-60-injured-loss.html |access-date=August 21, 2009 |archive-date=July 27, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180727151603/https://www.nytimes.com/1922/06/16/archives/400-buildings-burned-at-arverne-10000-made-homeless-60-injured-loss.html |url-status=live }}</ref> In 1928, a project to build 5,000 bungalows in Arverne was announced.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1928/07/27/archives/arverne-projects-are-announced.html|title=Arverne Projects Are Announced.|date=1928-07-27|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-24|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524014521/https://www.nytimes.com/1928/07/27/archives/arverne-projects-are-announced.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Decline ===
During the 1950s and 1960s, the advent of commercial [[jet airliner|jet]] air travel encouraged people to travel to distant destinations during the summer, rather than to local beaches and resorts. As a result, many of Arverne's summer bungalows became vacant. New York City's [[urban renewal]] projects of the 1960s leveled most of the summer resorts and some of the residences, many of which had been abandoned.<ref name="kensinger">{{cite web|url=http://kensinger.blogspot.com/2010/09/south-edgemere-wasteland.html|title=Nathan Kensinger Photography|work=kensinger.blogspot.com|access-date=29 May 2015|archive-date=29 March 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150329061838/http://kensinger.blogspot.com/2010/09/south-edgemere-wasteland.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1984/03/11/realestate/city-opens-its-biggest-plot-in-arverne-to-development.html|title=City Opens Its Biggest Plot, in Arverne, to Development|last=Sherman|first=Mark|date=1984-03-11|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-24|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524030853/https://www.nytimes.com/1984/03/11/realestate/city-opens-its-biggest-plot-in-arverne-to-development.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 1964, the New York City Planning Commission approved the designation of a {{Convert|302|acre|ha|abbr=|adj=on}} Arverne renewal area.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1964/11/26/archives/arverne-area-for-renewal.html|title=Arverne Area for Renewal|date=1964-11-26|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-24|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524014525/https://www.nytimes.com/1964/11/26/archives/arverne-area-for-renewal.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Two years later, the renewal area was expanded by 19 blocks.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1966/12/26/archives/renewal-expansion-sought-for-arverne.html|title=Renewal Expansion Sought for Arverne|date=1966-12-26|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-24|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524014524/https://www.nytimes.com/1966/12/26/archives/renewal-expansion-sought-for-arverne.html|url-status=live}}</ref> In expectation of the upcoming urban renewal, vacant bungalows were demolished.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1973/09/29/archives/eroded-rockaway-is-hoping-for-a-revival-eroded-rockaway-is-hoping.html|title=Eroded Rockaway Is Hoping for a Revival|last=Johnston|first=Laurie|date=1973-09-29|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-24|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524014527/https://www.nytimes.com/1973/09/29/archives/eroded-rockaway-is-hoping-for-a-revival-eroded-rockaway-is-hoping.html|url-status=live}}</ref> However, the renewal project was delayed, and a [[grand jury]] was convened to find the causes of the delay.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1966/12/08/archives/deteriorating-arverne-awaiting-urban-renewal-grand-jury-is.html|title=Deteriorating Arverne Awaiting Urban Renewal; Grand Jury Is Investigating Delays in Improving Area, an Old Vacation Spot|last=Roberts|first=Steven V.|date=1966-12-08|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-24|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524014526/https://www.nytimes.com/1966/12/08/archives/deteriorating-arverne-awaiting-urban-renewal-grand-jury-is.html|url-status=live}}</ref> A gap in funding from the U.S. federal government contributed to pressures to cancel the redevelopment.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1967/01/15/archives/delay-in-us-funds-affects-city-realty-projects-arverne-extension.html|title=Delay in U.S. Funds Affects City Realty Projects; Arverne Extension Barred --Razing Plan Slowed U.S. FUNDS TARDY, PROJECTS SLOWED|last=Bennett|first=Charles G.|date=1967-01-15|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-24|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524014523/https://www.nytimes.com/1967/01/15/archives/delay-in-us-funds-affects-city-realty-projects-arverne-extension.html|url-status=live}}</ref> In 1970, the city announced it would develop 970 apartments in Arverne by 1972.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1970/12/20/archives/arverne-housing-beset-by-delays-urban-development-plans-making-slow.html|title=Ărverne Housing Beset by Delays|date=1970-12-20|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-24|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524014530/https://www.nytimes.com/1970/12/20/archives/arverne-housing-beset-by-delays-urban-development-plans-making-slow.html|url-status=live}}</ref> By then, only about 100 of the original 900 bungalows remained. Controversy later arose when the city decided to place 100 [[mobile home]]s instead of permanent housing for low-income Puerto Ricans.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1971/04/18/archives/arverne-mirrors-renewal-woe.html|title=Arverne Mirrors Renewal Woe|last=Weisman|first=Steven R.|date=1971-04-18|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-24|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524014531/https://www.nytimes.com/1971/04/18/archives/arverne-mirrors-renewal-woe.html|url-status=live}}</ref> By 1973, Mayor [[John Lindsay]] was calling for 500 of 3,650 proposed housing units to be deleted from the Arverne redevelopment plan. As of yet, the 970 apartments in Arverne had not been developed.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1973/11/18/archives/city-offers-proposals-to-upgrade-rockaways-some-plans-fully-backed.html|title=City Offers Proposals To Upgrade Rockaways|date=1973-11-18|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-24|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524014520/https://www.nytimes.com/1973/11/18/archives/city-offers-proposals-to-upgrade-rockaways-some-plans-fully-backed.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

When the city re-opened Arverne to redevelopment in 1984, a {{Convert|123|acre|ha|abbr=|adj=on}} patch of Arverne only contained one structure: PS 106.<ref name=":0" /> In 1988, the administration of mayor [[Ed Koch]] started asking private developers to build on the site.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1988/11/20/realestate/perspectives-the-arverne-plan-oceanfront-site-terms-challenge-builders.html|title=PERSPECTIVES: The Arverne Plan; Oceanfront Site Terms Challenge Builders|last=Oser|first=Alan S.|date=1988-11-20|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-24|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524025342/https://www.nytimes.com/1988/11/20/realestate/perspectives-the-arverne-plan-oceanfront-site-terms-challenge-builders.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The Dubos Point Wildlife Sanctuary was designated that year as part of the plans for redevelopment.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2000/07/09/nyregion/neighborhood-report-arverne-wildlife-refuge-becomes-a-battleground-for-humans.html|title=NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: ARVERNE; Wildlife Refuge Becomes a Battleground for Humans|last=Day|first=Sherri|date=2000-07-09|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-24|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524023825/https://www.nytimes.com/2000/07/09/nyregion/neighborhood-report-arverne-wildlife-refuge-becomes-a-battleground-for-humans.html|url-status=live}}</ref> By 1991, the plans called for the construction of 7,500 apartments over 10 years at a cost of $1.5 billion.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/03/07/nyregion/after-20-lost-years-arverne-skeptically-awaits-renewal.html|title=After 20 Lost Years, Arverne Skeptically Awaits Renewal|last=Fried|first=Joseph P.|date=1991-03-07|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-24|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524023822/https://www.nytimes.com/1991/03/07/nyregion/after-20-lost-years-arverne-skeptically-awaits-renewal.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Finally, the late 1990s saw construction begin on a 322-unit development of two-family houses, the first such development in the 35-year-old Arverne renewal area.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1997/02/09/realestate/the-new-approach-in-arverne-incrementalism.html|title=The New Approach in Arverne: Incrementalism|last=Oser|first=Alan S.|date=1997-02-09|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-24|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524025346/https://www.nytimes.com/1997/02/09/realestate/the-new-approach-in-arverne-incrementalism.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The rest of the area's redevelopment was canceled after an economic downturn in the 1990s. People started dumping garbage in Dubos Point, to the consternation of residents.<ref name=":1" /> In 2003, ''[[The New York Times]]'' wrote:

{{Blockquote|For nearly four decades, grand plans were offered for the 52-block stretch from Beach 32nd to 84th Streets, between Rockaway Beach Boulevard and the boardwalk. [There was to be] a phalanx of mid- and high-rise condominium and rental apartment buildings, [as well as] more than $1 billion... enclosed amusement area on the Arverne site, to be called Destination Technodome, with rides, movie theaters, an indoor ski slope and a hotel.<ref name="nyt2003">{{cite web | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/12/07/realestate/in-rockaways-a-tide-is-coming-in.html?scp=1&sq=in%20rockaways%20a%20tide%20is%20coming | title=In Rockaways, a Tide Is Coming In | work=The New York Times | date=7 December 2003 | access-date=2 February 2015 | author=Steven Hevesi | archive-date=3 February 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150203064254/http://www.nytimes.com/2003/12/07/realestate/in-rockaways-a-tide-is-coming-in.html?scp=1&sq=in%20rockaways%20a%20tide%20is%20coming | url-status=live }}</ref>}}

=== Redevelopment ===
In the early 2000s, Mayor [[Michael Bloomberg]] started to revitalize Arverne with new housing and parks.<ref>{{cite news |title=Bloomberg's Big Day In Rockaway |newspaper=[[Wave of Long Island|The Wave]] |date=November 10, 2006 |url=http://www.arvernebythesea.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/01/11-10-06.pdf |access-date=May 11, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141023063739/http://www.arvernebythesea.com/wp-content/uploads/2012/01/11-10-06.pdf |archive-date=October 23, 2014 |url-status=dead }}</ref> This built upon a movement started in 1999, when 40 houses were built in the portion of the Arverne renewal area between Beach 59th and 61st Streets.<ref name="nyt2003" />

{{As of|2003}}, {{convert|97|acre|ha}} of the "Edgemere Urban Renewal Area"  was to have 400 houses built within it.<ref name="kensinger" /> Of these, {{convert|47|acre|ha}} would be houses, {{convert|35|acre|ha}} would be a nature preserve, and {{convert|15|acre|ha}} would be a segment of preserved dunes on the beach.<ref name="nyc.gov">[http://www.nyc.gov/html/hpd/html/developers/large-scale-arverne.shtml Large-Scale Development: Arverne] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150203053208/http://www.nyc.gov/html/hpd/html/developers/large-scale-arverne.shtml|date=February 3, 2015}}, nyc.gov</ref>

Arverne and other parts of the Rockaways increasingly got attention and press as the redevelopment of the beachfront continued.<ref>{{cite news |title=Top 10 neighborhoods for real estate investment |newspaper=[[New York Daily News]] |date=August 10, 2012 |url=http://www.arvernebythesea.com/new-york-daily-news-top-10-neighborhoods-for-real-estate-investment/ |access-date=Oct 15, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120924074743/http://www.arvernebythesea.com/new-york-daily-news-top-10-neighborhoods-for-real-estate-investment/ |archive-date=September 24, 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref> To improve pedestrian accessibility, a section of Rockaway Freeway beneath the station was closed to through traffic<ref>''Rockaway Wave'' Editorial “Closing Rockaway Freeway a Plus for Rockaway” December 24, 2004 http://www.rockawave.com/news/2004-12-24/Editorial/035.html {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161104022434/http://www.rockawave.com/news/2004-12-24/Editorial/035.html |date=2016-11-04 }}</ref> and the Beach 67th Street–Gaston Avenue station was renamed Beach 67th Street–Arverne by the Sea as a symbolic recognition of the neighborhood's rebirth as a residential area and a summer waterfront destination.

One of the largest developments, the 2,300-unit Arverne by the Sea, first opened to residents in 2006.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/06/25/nyregion/thecity/waiting-for-high-tide.html|title=Waiting for High Tide|last=Vandam|first=Jeff|date=2006-06-25|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-24|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524025340/https://www.nytimes.com/2006/06/25/nyregion/thecity/waiting-for-high-tide.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Despite an economic downturn in 2008, the $1 billion development was mostly successful, and units sold at prices of up to $1 million.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/09/14/realestate/14post.html|title=Sitting Pretty by the Sea|last=Hughes|first=C. J.|date=2008-09-12|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-24|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524014519/https://www.nytimes.com/2008/09/14/realestate/14post.html|url-status=live}}</ref> By 2012, Arverne by the Sea was largely developed.<ref>{{cite news |title=Rockaway Beach becomes 'Hipster Hamptons |newspaper=[[Newsday]] |date=August 13, 2012 |url=http://www.arvernebythesea.com/rockaway-beach-becomes-hipster-hamptons/ |access-date=Oct 15, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304045445/http://arvernebythesea.com/rockaway-beach-becomes-hipster-hamptons/ |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |url-status=dead }}</ref> New restaurants and retail establishments arrived as part of an effort to make shopping available to local residents at a hub near the [[Beach 67th Street station]].<ref>[https://www.rockawave.com/articles/arverne-amenities-lost-at-sea/ "Arverne Amenities Lost At Sea?"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190727191216/https://www.rockawave.com/articles/arverne-amenities-lost-at-sea/ |date=2019-07-27 }}, ''The Wave'', August 14, 2009. Accessed January 8, 2024.</ref><ref>[https://www.rockawave.com/articles/super-stop-and-shop-takes-shape/ "Super Stop And Shop Takes Shape"] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190817182340/https://www.rockawave.com/articles/super-stop-and-shop-takes-shape/ |date=2019-08-17 }}, ''The Wave'', April 16, 2010. Accessed January 8, 2024. "The Super Stop and Shop at Arverne By The Sea is beginning to take shape as construction continues at the site on Rockaway Beach Boulevard and Beach 73 Street. The eagerly anticipated supermarket is expected to be completed in time for Thanksgiving. The store will be built in conjunction with a new retail transit hub at the Beach 67 Street train station."</ref> Phase I was completed in 2011; Phase II was begun in 2006.<ref name="nyc.gov" />

In October 2018, construction began on the Tides development. By mid-2019, Arverne was undergoing gentrification as new businesses were opening in the area, which was still over 60% Black and 20% Hispanic/Latino.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/05/17/nyregion/arverne-rockaway-beach.html|title=Are Surfer Cafes and Green Markets What a Working-Class Beach Neighborhood Needs?|last=Branch|first=Kate|date=2019-05-17|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-05-24|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524023823/https://www.nytimes.com/2019/05/17/nyregion/arverne-rockaway-beach.html|url-status=live}}</ref> According to census data from the 2019 [[American Community Survey]], the Black population declined as a percentage of the population to 56.8%.

==Education==
The [[New York City Department of Education]] operates Arverne's public schools. These schools include PS/MS 42 Robert Vernam School and PS 183 Dr. Richard R. Green.

The [[Queens Public Library]] operates the Arverne branch at 312 Beach 54th Street.<ref>{{cite web | title=Branch Detailed Info: Arverne | website=Queens Public Library | url=https://www.queenslibrary.org/about-us/locations/Arverne/ | access-date=March 7, 2019 | archive-date=October 16, 2019 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191016212206/https://www.queenslibrary.org/about-us/locations/arverne | url-status=live }}</ref>

==Housing==

==Transportation==
The [[New York City Subway]]'s [[Beach 67th Street station|Beach 67th Street]] and [[Beach 60th Street station]]s, served by the {{NYCS trains|Rockaway}}, are located in Arverne.<ref>{{NYCS const|map}}</ref> The {{NYC bus link|Q22|Q52 SBS|QM15|QM17|prose=y}} [[MTA Bus]] routes also serve the neighborhood.<ref>{{Cite NYC bus map|Q}}</ref>

==Parks==
The {{Convert|8.6|acre|ha|abbr=|adj=on}} [[Kohlreiter Square]] is located on the north side of [[Rockaway Freeway]] between Beach 67th and Beach 69th Streets.

There are three wildlife sanctuaries in Arverne, all part of the [[Gateway National Recreation Area]]. The Dubos Point Wildlife Sanctuary is  northeast of the intersection of Da Costa Avenue and Beach 65th Street, fronting [[Jamaica Bay]]. It was acquired in 1988 and named for microbiologist Dr. [[René Dubos]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/dubos-point-wildlife-sanctuary/history|title=Dubos Point Wildlife Sanctuary Highlights : NYC Parks|website=www.nycgovparks.org|access-date=2019-05-24|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524014522/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/dubos-point-wildlife-sanctuary/history|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> At the northwest corner of Arverne is Brant Point Wildlife Sanctuary, located west of Beach 72nd Street and north of Hillmeyer Avenue on Jamaica Bay. It was transferred to the jurisdiction of the [[New York City Department of Parks and Recreation]] in 1992.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/brant-point-wildlife-sanctuary/history|title=Brant Point Wildlife Sanctuary Highlights : NYC Parks|website=www.nycgovparks.org|access-date=2019-05-24|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524014523/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/brant-point-wildlife-sanctuary/history|url-status=live}}</ref> A third sanctuary, Vernam Barbadoes Preserve, is on Terrapeninsula, a peninsula between two inlets of Jamaica Bay west of Beach 75th Street and north of Amstel Boulevard. It was designated as the "Terrapeninsula Preserve" in 1997, but is commonly referred to as Vernam.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/vernam-barbadoes-peninsula/history|title=Vernam Barbadoes Peninsula Highlights : NYC Parks|website=www.nycgovparks.org|access-date=2019-05-24|archive-date=2019-05-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190524014521/https://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/vernam-barbadoes-peninsula/history|url-status=live}}</ref>
